title: The mud mosque of Djenné
hookLine: the Great Mosque of mud, replastered by the whole town

lines: A WHOLE MOSQUE GETS A NEW SKIN.
cards: Before dawn, drums. Then people pour into the square: boys with baskets of wet mud on their heads, women and girls carrying water from the river, old men giving orders, masons up on the walls.

Bundles of palm wood stick out of the building like the bristles of a brush, and men climb them like ladders, smoothing fresh mud over the walls with their hands. By the end of the day a whole mosque has a new skin.
This is Djenné, an old town on a river in Mali, and its Great Mosque is built of earth. Today: the mud mosque of Djenné.

teach.b: Mud is a strange thing to build a great mosque from: sun-dried bricks, held together and coated with more mud, mixed with things like rice husks so it holds. It is cool inside in the heat. But mud has an enemy: rain.

teach.h: THE RAINS WASH THE WALLS AWAY.
teach.b: The rainy season washes some of the walls away. So, by long custom, the town comes out together and puts it back. The masons lead; their skill is handed down in families.
Everyone else carries. Those palm sticks poking out of the walls aren't decoration. They're scaffolding that never comes down.

teach.h: A PALACE TORN DOWN FOR A MOSQUE.
teach.b: The chronicler al-Sa'di tells how the town's first mosque came to be: a ruler of Djenné became Muslim, tore down his own palace, and built a mosque on the site.
The building that stands today is not that first one, but it stands in its line. The Qur'an has a line about who looks after the houses of God.
In Pickthall's translation: "He only shall tend Allah's sanctuaries who believeth in Allah and the Last Day."
And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that whoever builds a mosque for God, God builds the like of it for them in Paradise. In Djenné, building is never finished.

teach.h: THE MOSQUE WOULD MELT WITHOUT THE TOWN.
teach.b: The mosque would melt without the town, and the town gathers because of the mosque.
Nobody owns the job. Everyone owns a basket.

how: In Djenné the townspeople gather for the replastering of the Great Mosque, led by the masons, with young people carrying mud and others bringing water.

games.q: the rains have washed the walls of your town's mud mosque thinner. what does the town do?
o: hire a crew from outside to fix it.
cover it in something that never needs fixing.
everyone comes out together and replasters it by hand.
games.why: by long custom the whole town turns out: masons on the walls, young people with baskets of mud, others bringing water. the mosque needs the town.

practice: Think of something shared that is wearing thin: a fence between neighbors, a family tradition nobody has organized lately, a room at your mosque, church or community center.
Ask who else cares about it, and what one basket of mud you could carry. If you pray, ask God's blessing on the work; if not, simply picture it finished.

wordCard.voice: Djenné. The Malian town whose Great Mosque of earth is washed by the rains and replastered by the whole town. Today's word.
